learning.title: A destructive red-proof pollutes the test database: reset it before trusting the green that follows
learning.body:
Found by qa-qa gating #517 at 45ca3cc07 (2026-11-17). Red-proving a reaper by broadening its delete to `where part.part_number > 0` wipes every row in bakery.blob_upload_parts. Restoring the source and re-running the same suite then gave 0 passed / 27 failed with:
CreateSuperuserError: AUTH_BOOTSTRAP_CONFLICT
The test-database reset (BAKERY_TEST_DATABASE_RESET_CONFIRMATION= RESET_BAKERY_TEST_DATABASE) does not clear the superuser the wiped run left behind, so the next run cannot bootstrap and every test fails at setup. The code was correct the whole time; the red was pollution.
The trap: a destructive red-proof produces a red that is not the code, and the green you run afterwards to prove you restored correctly is not green either. Both readings are wrong in the same direction - you either chase a regression that does not exist or, worse, accept a polluted run as evidence.
Rule: after any red-proof that deletes or rewrites rows (broadened delete, dropped predicate, truncated table), drop and recreate the database before running the suite you intend to trust:
docker exec <project>-postgres-1 psql -U postgres -d postgres \ -c "drop database if exists bakery with (force);" \ -c "create database bakery owner bakery;"
Note the owner: the application role (bakery) cannot create databases ("permission denied to create database"), so the recreate must run as the postgres superuser even though the drop succeeds as bakery.
Same shape as the night's other findings: a green that is not green and a red that is not the code. The counter is the same - ask what the failure would look like if the thing under test were fine, and if the answer is "exactly this", suspect the instrument before the code.
SHARPER RULE, from the author breaking it the same night: a red-proof measurement is only valid on a database that has not already been through the red-proof. The first run is clean; every run after it is polluted. So it is one destructive red-proof per fresh database, and a second measurement needs a recreated database first, not a reset.
The instance: qa-qa reported "0 passed / 14 failed" as a counter-example to dev-server's "8 passed / 5 failed" for the same broadening, in the same message that argued a number depending on the environment is not evidence. The 0/14 was the second run in a sequence and was pure pollution. Re-measured on a fresh database it was 8 passed / 6 failed - the 8 matching dev-server exactly, the 1-test gap being environment. The counter-example was not a measurement at all, and the tell ("name what would have to be true for this to be valid") would have caught it if applied to the reporter's own claim rather than only to the other party's.
